idiom_name: runtime predicate dispatch: typeof/instanceof checks, discriminated unions, dispatch objects
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no language-level overloading: two declarations of the same name in a scope mean the second replaces the first, and there is no signature-based dispatch, so nothing can be selected from a type at load time. What replaces the classic structure: runtime checks on values (typeof, instanceof, a discriminant field, Array.isArray) inside a single function, or polymorphic methods on the objects, or a dispatch object/Map keyed by a type or kind. The classic form has no counterpart here; the closest analogue is a Map from constructor to implementation, which is a runtime table and pays a lookup per call.
pitfalls: typeof is not a type test: typeof null === 'object', arrays, dates and errors are all 'object', and cross-realm values fail instanceof - so a hand-written ladder tends to have branches that never fire or fire wrongly.
Repeated declarations silently overwrite instead of overloading, so a 'ladder' written as several function declarations loses every branch but the last, with no warning at parse time.
Dispatch keyed on constructor or prototype breaks under subclassing, proxies and structural cloning (structuredClone, JSON round-trips), where the tag value is lost even though the shape survives.
sources: Function Overloading in JavaScript: Practical Patterns (no signature-based dispatch; later declarations overwrite; TypeScript overload signatures are compile-time only), https://thelinuxcode.com/function-overloading-in-javascript-practical-patterns-for-2026/
Reginald Braithwaite, Greenspunning Predicate and Multiple Dispatch in JavaScript, https://raganwald.com/2014/06/23/multiple-dispatch.html
alternative: Put the operation on the objects themselves (polymorphic methods, the 'replace conditional with polymorphism' refactoring) or key a dispatch map/object by a discriminant field; for genuine multiple dispatch use a predicate-dispatch helper or a multi-method library. There is no compile-time binding in JavaScript, so a tag cannot select an implementation before the program runs.
